title: The loon
hook: he chased a loon on the pond that laughed and dived (Walden 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ant war: red against black on the woodpile, and Thoreau stopping everything to watch. Your line was the small war.

A calm afternoon in fall. The pond is flat as glass. Thoreau is out in his boat, and not far off sits a loon, a big black-and-white diving bird. He paddles toward it. It dives. He stops, scanning the water, guessing where it will come up. It surfaces somewhere else entirely, far off, sometimes behind him. And then it laughs, that long, wild call rolling across the water. So he picks a new direction and tries again. And again.
screen: `A CALM POND, A LOON.` → `IT DIVES.` → `IT LAUGHS.`

segments.voice: First, the game. In Brute Neighbors, Thoreau tells the chase move by move, and calls it what it is: "a pretty game, played on the smooth surface of the pond, a man against a loon." Notice the word game. He isn't hunting it or trying to hurt it. He wants to outguess it, and he keeps losing. Second, the cleverness. The loon picks the widest stretch of water to dive in, stays down long, swims far underneath, and comes up where he least expected. This is the man who sounded the whole pond with a line and stone. He knows this water, and a bird still runs rings around him. Third, the laughter. Each time it comes up, it calls, and Thoreau hears the call as a laugh, wild and unearthly. He wonders if the bird is laughing at him. He doesn't sound offended. He sounds delighted. Fourth, the ending. The wind rises, a light rain begins, and Thoreau half-jokes that it's as if the loon had called on its god for help, and the god had answered. He gives up, and the loon is left out on the water, unbeaten. There's a kind of freedom in that ending. Not everything has to be caught, solved or won. Some things are better for being wilder than you are, and the best you can do is enjoy the game.
screen: `A MAN AGAINST A LOON.` · `IT COMES UP WHERE YOU DON'T LOOK.` · `A LAUGH ACROSS THE WATER.` · then, large: `THE LOON STAYS UNBEATEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you can't control or predict, the weather, a cat, a small child, your own wandering mind, and let it be the loon: watch it dive and come up somewhere else, and notice the urge to chase it down. For this one sit, let it win. If your attention wanders, don't drag it back hard; smile at where it surfaced, and come back gently.
The loon. The bird that dived, surfaced far away, and laughed, in Thoreau's pretty game of a man against a loon. Today's word.
Your line: the laughing loon. Some games are better lost. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Brute Neighbors often enjoy the loon chase as a picture of meeting something wild with play rather than control, and of taking defeat with good humor.

He was hunting it for food, and called it a game to hide his frustration.
He caught it in the end, but let it go, so he called the whole thing a game.

notes: Confirm exact wording: 'It was a pretty game, played on the smooth surface of the pond, a man against a loon.'

Paraphrased: the loon's 'demoniac laughter', its 'unearthly howl', Thoreau's sense that it 'laughed in derision of my efforts', and the closing image of the east wind and drizzling rain as if the loon's prayer were answered. Confirm.
The text sets the chase on a calm October afternoon; the script says 'a calm afternoon in fall' to avoid a date claim beyond the text.
'He knows this water' is the narrator's emphasis, linking to the sounding in The Pond in Winter; trim if a reviewer prefers.
The description of a loon as a 'big black-and-white diving bird' is general natural history, not from the text.
